clue.text: An engrossing game

parts.note: surface reading: a game so absorbing that it holds the players' attention
setter's reading: to engross is also to buy up the whole supply of something, which is what players of this board game try to do with property

explanation.walkthrough: Engross has an old commercial sense, to corner a market, so the game is one about cornering the market.
explanation.definitionFit: The board game's aim is exclusive control of property, and exclusive control of a market is the economic sense of the word.

clue.text: Knutsford, literally where Conservative ran for the money in Harrods

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
taken as written
taken as written
d was the symbol for the old British penny, and it is also the D inside Harrods

explanation.surface: A Tory politician races round the luxury London department store Harrods hunting for cash in Knutsford.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Gaskell's novel Cranford is modelled on the Cheshire town of Knutsford, so the book's town is Knutsford in literature. Harrods is a famous London department store.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaskell based her fictional town on Knutsford, where she grew up, so the novel's setting is that real place in literary disguise.

clue.text: When fellow leaves for Spain, barely drunk

indicators.note: one letter departs to make way for another, so the first named swaps into the second's place

parts.note: taken as written
F is the abbreviation for fellow
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: A man heads off to Spain on holiday, having had barely a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: In BARELY the E (Spain) gives way to F (fellow), giving BARFLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A drunk, the noun, is someone who drinks too much, and a barfly is a regular heavy drinker who haunts bars.

clue.text: Proclaims, but doesn't begin to intrude in, standing orders

indicators.note: something intruding pushes its way inside another thing

parts.note: to proclaim is to state

indicators.note: a word that fails to begin has lost its opening letter

parts.note: taken as written, then losing its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone announces rules while saying they do not mean to interfere with established procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make 'but' read as a conjunction, yet it is the fodder that loses its head.
explanation.definitionFit: Statutes are laws laid down by a legislature that remain in force, which is what standing orders are.

clue.text: Hush! It's Newman's "Gone With the Wind"

parts.words: Hush! It's Newman's "Gone With the Wind"
parts.note: surface reading: an announcement calling for quiet about a famous film
setter's reading: one whose wind has gone, that is, someone out of breath; Hush recalls a famous poetic phrase pairing the answer with hush

explanation.surface: An usher calls for silence before a screening of a classic film.
explanation.walkthrough: The film title is read literally: someone whose wind has gone. 'Hush' recalls the famous 'breathless hush in the Close tonight' of Newbolt's poem Vitai Lampada.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone whose wind has gone is winded, panting, unable to catch their breath.

clue.text: No veal raised in this small container

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something turns it upside down, so it is read from the bottom

parts.note: taken as written
veal is the meat of a calf

explanation.surface: A warning that no veal is ever kept or served in this little dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A flacon is a small stoppered bottle, especially for perfume, so it is a little vessel for holding liquid.

clue.text: See 11
Community work in the French department

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits within its boundaries

parts.note: the Eure is a department of Normandy
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A community project carried out in a French administrative region.
explanation.walkthrough: The European Community was the earlier name for what became the European Union.
explanation.definitionFit: The European Community was the political grouping of the continent's nations, so the continent's name stands for it.

clue.text: See 10
He was, some said of the Skye-bound lad, a king having no trouble failing

definitions.text: He was, some said of the Skye-bound lad

indicators.note: something failing is breaking down, so these letters collapse and are rebuilt

parts.note: R, from rex, is a king
taken as written

explanation.surface: People said a king who sailed off to Skye had an easy time of failing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Skye Boat Song carries 'the lad that's born to be king over the sea to Skye': Bonnie Prince Charlie, the Jacobite pretender, who failed to win the throne.
explanation.definitionFit: The song says Charles Edward Stuart was destined for kingship, which is what being destined to reign means.

clue.text: Caution opening game plan: author-chefs carry it out

indicators.note: letters carried out are taken apart and set down in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: Cookery writers follow the warning that heads a recipe for cooking game.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying is often wrongly credited to the cookery writers Hannah Glasse or Mrs Beeton, so the author-chefs really do carry it out.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb warns that you need the essential thing in hand before planning, and it supposedly opened a recipe for jugged hare.

clue.text: Something fishy about this duck? Try some old port

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... duck is not a bird but a dried fish
second meaning: the former name of Mumbai, India's great port

explanation.surface: A diner suspects the duck is off and suggests a glass of vintage port instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old port' looks like a drink to try, but it is a city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian city now called Mumbai was known by this name for centuries, and a dried lizardfish takes its name too.

clue.text: Cutting communication between landowners and ramblers?

definitions.text: Cutting communication between landowners and ramblers?

parts.note: a cutting remark is barbed
a wire is a telegram

explanation.surface: Farmers and walkers have stopped speaking to each other over a right of way.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the spiked fencing that literally cuts off walkers from a landowner's fields.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiked fence strands keep walkers off private farmland, so they are the sharp-edged barrier between property owners and hikers.

clue.text: Taking it on the chin, lodger goes out, giving us the key

indicators.note: going outside means wrapping round whatever else is named

parts.note: PG, paying guest, is a lodger
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tenant who has taken a beating moves out and hands back the house key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking it on the chin' reads as an idiom for enduring blows, but it means IT placed on CHIN. 'the key' is musical, not a door key.
explanation.definitionFit: A singer or instrument sounding the starting note sets the musical register for everyone else.

clue.text: Fool I see in Richard's house — or Denmark's?

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside its letters

parts.note: Richard III belonged to the House of York
taken as written
the letter C is pronounced like see, a standard crossword substitution

explanation.surface: Someone spots a court jester at an English royal house, or perhaps at the Danish court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or Denmark's?' adds that this fool belonged to the Danish court: in Hamlet, the prince holds the skull of the old king's jester.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the dead court jester in Shakespeare's play, and jesters were professional fools.

clue.text: Po-faced lexicography here?

parts.note: surface reading: dictionary-making done with a solemn, humourless expression
setter's reading: a po is a chamber pot, and the answer is both chamber pots and a famous dictionary publisher

explanation.walkthrough: A po is British slang for a chamber pot. The answer is also the Edinburgh publisher of the Chambers Dictionary, long beloved of crossword setters.
explanation.definitionFit: The publisher's name is the plural of a word for bedroom, and a chamber pot is a po, so dictionaries and pots meet here.

clue.text: Elevation of priest into a division of the church

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something put into another goes inside it

parts.note: a sect is a breakaway religious group
P is the abbreviation for priest

explanation.surface: A priest is promoted within a breakaway branch of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevation' suggests promotion, but it is the architect's word for one face of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: In architecture an elevation is a drawing of one face of a building, and the direction a building faces is its outlook.

clue.text: The direction of Westerns

parts.note: surface reading: the way cowboy films are directed by film-makers
setter's reading: the way pointed out to a sheriff's posse in a Western, as in the stock line

explanation.walkthrough: In cowboy films someone points and says the outlaws went 'that way', drawled as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the stock pointing-out of where the fugitives rode off in cowboy films.

clue.text: A two-master turning south invariably

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: turning round makes a word run the other way

parts.note: a yawl is a sailing boat with two masts
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A twin-masted sailing boat always heads south.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done invariably happens every time without exception, which is the meaning of the adverb.

clue.text: Still beyond infinity

parts.note: beyond in time means after
infinity is everything, all there is

explanation.surface: A Buzz Lightyear-style rallying cry: to infinity and further still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adjective for calm, but it is the adverb meaning nevertheless.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs of concession meaning nevertheless or in spite of what has been said.

clue.text: False bread maker …

parts.note: surface reading: a baker who makes fake loaves
setter's reading: bread is slang for money, so the maker of false money is a counterfeiter

explanation.walkthrough: Bread is old slang for money; the ellipsis leads on to the next clue, which really is about baking.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterfeiter produces fake banknotes, and bread is a slang word for cash.

clue.text: Public transport without conductor

parts.note: a bus is public transport
bar means except, without

explanation.surface: A bus running with no conductor on board to collect fares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conductor' wants to be the bus conductor of the surface, but it is electrical.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a thick metal strip in switchgear that carries current to several circuits, an electrical conductor.

clue.text: … one could prove it here

parts.note: surface reading: a place where someone could demonstrate the truth of something
setter's reading: dough is left to prove, to rise, before baking

explanation.walkthrough: To prove dough is to let it rise; following the counterfeit bread maker of the previous clue, this is where real bread is made.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaves are made in this shop, and leaving dough to rise is called proving it.

clue.text: Exhausted knight, holding mirror to naked duchess, might get nowhere

indicators.note: one thing holding another has it inside

parts.note: exhausted and haggard: drawn
K is an abbreviation for knight

indicators.note: a mirror image runs the other way, so this word is read backwards

parts.note: the Duchess of Alba is said to have posed for Goya's nude painting, the Naked Maja

explanation.surface: A worn-out knight holds up a mirror to an unclothed noblewoman and may get nowhere with her.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to search or try and find nothing, which is failing to make any progress.

clue.text: Constable positioned at this level-crossing?

parts.note: level ground is flat
a ford is a shallow river crossing

explanation.surface: A police officer stationed at a railway level crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable' is not a policeman but John Constable, who painted Flatford Mill in Suffolk and its ford on the River Stour.
explanation.definitionFit: The painter John Constable set up his easel at this Suffolk hamlet, which really has a shallow river crossing.

clue.text: See 2 and 24 across
Servant paid on demand?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a carrier or attendant, especially in colonial India
second meaning: a cheque or note payable to the holder is paid to whoever presents it

explanation.walkthrough: Banknotes promise to 'pay the bearer on demand', so the holder is the one paid.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrying attendant is one sense; the person who presents a banknote and receives its value is the other.

clue.text: Like the Brontes? That's so right! One's spoken about!

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
oral means spoken
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An enthusiast cries that the Brontes fit the bill exactly, since people talk about them.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte, Emily and Anne Bronte were sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to or like a sister, and the three Brontes were famous literary siblings.
